messages.content:
Rate the following clinical vignette:

Kenji speaks about his life before the storm with a kind of detached reverence, as if describing a photograph of someone else's family. He was home for the holidays, a rare break from his demanding job as a UX designer in the city. He remembers the humidity, the smell of his grandmother's cooking, and the specific shade of green on the palm leaves outside her window. He was proud of his work, of the clean, logical user journeys he designed. His world was one of predictable paths and intuitive interfaces, a place where a user could always find their way home with a few simple clicks.

That world was washed away in less than a day. The typhoon wasn't just a storm; it was a dismantling of reality. He talks about the wind first, a sound that wasn't a whistle but a physical roar that vibrated in his bones. Then the water, rising with an impossible speed, turning the familiar street into a brown, churning river. He and his father were trying to get his grandmother, who refused to leave her home, onto the roof. He remembers the feel of her hand, wrinkled and surprisingly strong, slipping from his grasp as a surge of water slammed against the house. He remembers the silence that followed the roar, a silence filled only by the relentless sound of the rain.

It has been eight months. Back in his minimalist city apartment, Kenji tries to reconstruct the logic that once governed his life. But the chaos of the flood has seeped into everything. He is praised at work for his meticulous attention to detail, but his colleagues don't see the compulsion behind it. He spends hours adjusting the alignment of a button by a single pixel, an attempt to exert control over a universe that has proven to be violently arbitrary. A sudden downpour outside his office window can leave him breathless, his monitor blurring as the memory of rising water fills his vision. He feels a cold dread pool in his stomach, the same feeling he had standing on that roof, watching the debris float by.

Sleep offers no escape. He often jolts awake from nightmares of the flood, his sheets damp with sweat, the phantom sensation of his grandmother's hand slipping away still tingling in his palm. During the day, he is a ghost haunting his own life. He sits in meetings, nodding along as his team discusses user engagement, but the words are just noise. He feels a profound disconnect from his friends and their seemingly trivial concerns-dating apps, weekend plans, office politics. How can he care about any of that when he knows how fragile it all is? He feels an immense, suffocating guilt, a constant loop of "what ifs" playing in his mind. If he had just been stronger, if he had held on tighter, if he had forced her to leave earlier.

He avoids calling his family, the conversations strained and heavy with what is left unsaid. He has stopped checking the news, terrified of seeing another story about a natural disaster. The sound of a passing ambulance or a car backfiring makes him flinch violently, his heart hammering against his ribs. He feels constantly on edge, scanning every room for exits, every skyline for storm clouds. He exists in two timelines: the clean, ordered world of his design work, and the churning, muddy chaos of the moment the water took everything. He is an expert at designing clear paths for others, but he cannot find a way forward for himself.

This clearly satisfies DSM-5 Criterion A.
